title: React Hooks
subtitle: The Superpowers of Modern React - useState, useEffect & Beyond
description: Master Hooks rules, useState deep dive, useEffect for data fetching like your Firebase dashboard, dependency array, cleanup, useRef, and build real features: live timer, auto-save, API calls.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: Why Hooks? The Story Before and After

Hey! Before 2019, if you wanted state or lifecycle (like fetching data when component loads), you HAD to use Class components with this.state and componentDidMount - complicated, confusing this keyword, lots of code. Functional components were dumb - they could only show UI, no state, no side effects.

In 2019, React team introduced Hooks. Hooks = functions that let functional components use state, lifecycle, and other React features. Now functional components can do EVERYTHING class components did, but simpler, cleaner, no this. That's why your dashboard you gave me uses functional components + hooks - it's modern standard.

Today you master 2 most important hooks that power 90% of your Lesson 10 final app: useState (we started in Lesson 4, now deep dive) and useEffect (for data fetching, timers, saving to Firebase). These two hooks alone build your entire dashboard loading logic!
INTERACTIVE RULE: Before we start, open Menu > Practical > React. We will test every hook live. Don't skip.
PAGE 2: The 2 Golden Rules of Hooks - Break Them and App Crashes

Rule 1: Only call hooks at TOP LEVEL of your component. Never inside if, for, nested function, or after return. Why? React relies on order of hooks to track state. If you call useState inside if, order changes, React gets confused, bug!
Rule 2: Only call hooks INSIDE React functional components or custom hooks. Never inside normal JavaScript function, class, or outside component. Hooks need React context to work.

blocks.title: Example 1: Rules of Hooks - Wrong vs Correct (MOST COMMON INTERVIEW QUESTION)
blocks.output: Correct version always works, Wrong versions cause 'Rendered more hooks than during previous render' error

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You have a component that shows user profile only if user is logged in. You wrote: if (loggedIn) { const [profile, setProfile] = useState(null); }. What happens?
options: Works fine
Crashes with 'Rendered more hooks than previous render' because hook order changes when loggedIn changes
Profile will be undefined always
Hooks can be inside if conditions
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! This is the #1 hooks bug in real jobs. Always call hooks at top, outside any condition.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Rule 1: Never inside if/for. Call useState at top always, then use its value inside if.
blocks.reasoning: Hooks order must be consistent across renders - React's core mechanism.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You have const [user, setUser] = useState({name: 'Ama', xp: 100}). You want to update xp to 150 but keep name. Which is correct?
options: user.xp = 150; // Direct mutation
setUser({ xp: 150 }) // Only xp, name lost!
setUser({...user, xp: 150 }) // Spread old, overwrite xp
setUser(user.xp + 50)
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Spread...user keeps all old properties, then xp: 150 overwrites only xp. Immutable update pattern.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Never mutate directly. Always create new object: setUser({...user, xp: 150}) - spread keeps name, xp updates.
blocks.reasoning: Immutable updates are required for React to detect changes and re-render.

blocks.text: PAGE 4: useEffect - The Side Effect Manager (Most Important Hook After useState)

State is for data inside component. But what about things OUTSIDE component? Fetching lessons from Firebase, setting timer, saving XP to localStorage, changing document title. These are Side Effects - things that affect outside world. useEffect handles side effects.

Think: Your component is a person. useState is person's memory. useEffect is person's actions that affect outside world - like calling API (phone call), setting interval (alarm), saving to database (writing diary). useEffect runs AFTER component renders.

Syntax: useEffect(() => { // side effect code }, [dependencies]). Dependencies array tells React WHEN to run effect. No array = run after every render. [] empty = run only once after first render (mount). [xp] = run when xp changes.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: In your dashboard, you have loading spinner that shows while fetching from Firebase, then shows lessons. Which useEffect dependency makes fetch run only once on page load?
options: useEffect(() => { fetch() }) // No dependency array - runs after every render - infinite loop!
useEffect(() => { fetch() }, []) // Empty array - runs only once after first mount - CORRECT for initial fetch
useEffect(() => { fetch() }, [lessons]) // Runs every time lessons changes - also infinite loop!
You don't need useEffect for fetching
blocks.correctFeedback: YES! [] empty = mount only once. That's your dashboard's loading logic. No array = infinite loop bug!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Empty [] = run once on mount - perfect for initial Firebase fetch. No array = runs every render = infinite loop fetching!
blocks.reasoning: Dependency array controls when effect runs - critical for data fetching.

blocks.text: PAGE 5: useEffect Dependencies - The Tricky Part Made Simple

Dependency array is like a watch list. React watches those values. If any value in array changes since last render, effect runs again. If empty [], nothing to watch, so runs only once. If [xp], runs when xp changes. If no array at all, React doesn't know what to watch, so runs after EVERY render.

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You want document title to show 'React Course - 3/10 completed'. Title should update whenever completed count changes. How?
options: useEffect(() => { document.title = `React Course - ${completed}/10` }, [completed]) // Runs when completed changes
useEffect(() => { document.title =... }, []) // Empty array - title never updates after first time
Set document.title directly in component body without useEffect
You cannot change document title in React
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Dependency [completed] means title updates whenever completed changes. That's reactive!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Put completed in dependency array so effect re-runs when completed count changes and updates title.
blocks.reasoning: Dependency array makes effects reactive to specific state changes.

blocks.text: PAGE 6: Cleanup - The Most Overlooked But Critical Part

What if you set an interval timer with setInterval in useEffect, but user navigates to another page? Interval keeps running, memory leak, app slows! Cleanup function solves this: Return a function from useEffect that cleans up - clearInterval, remove event listener, cancel fetch. Cleanup runs before next effect and when component unmounts.

blocks.title: Example 6: Cleanup - Timer and Event Listener (Real App Need)
blocks.output:
Time: 10:30:45 AM [Hide Clock]
Click Hide -> interval stops (cleanup works)

blocks.question: APPLICATION: You added window.addEventListener('resize',...) in useEffect to track screen size. User navigates away but resize listener still fires and causes error. What did you miss?
options: You forgot cleanup - return () => window.removeEventListener('resize',...) in useEffect
You need to add more event listeners
useEffect doesn't need cleanup for event listeners
Resize listener auto-removes itself
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Every addEventListener in useEffect needs removeEventListener in cleanup return. Otherwise memory leak!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Cleanup is mandatory for subscriptions: intervals, event listeners, WebSocket connections. Return cleanup function.
blocks.reasoning: Cleanup prevents memory leaks - essential for production apps like your Code Academy app.

blocks.text: PAGE 7: useRef - The Secret Hook for DOM and Values That Don't Trigger Re-render

useRef is like a box that holds value but changing it does NOT trigger re-render. Two uses: 1. Access DOM element directly (focus input, measure div). 2. Store value that persists across renders but doesn't need to trigger re-render (like previous value, timer id). Syntax: const inputRef = useRef(null); <input ref={inputRef} />; then inputRef.current.focus().

blocks.question: FINAL APPLICATION: Your dashboard code has: const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true) and useEffect with [] that fetches Firebase. Why do you need isMounted flag and cleanup?
options: You don't need it, it's extra code
If user navigates away before fetch finishes, component unmounts, but fetch tries to setState on unmounted component causing memory leak warning - isMounted prevents that
isMounted makes fetch faster
Firebase requires isMounted flag
blocks.correctFeedback: BINGO! This is production-level bug fix - prevents 'Can't perform React state update on unmounted component' error. Senior devs always add this!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Cleanup with isMounted prevents state update after unmount - essential when fetching data that takes time.
blocks.reasoning: Handling async operations with cleanup is crucial for real Firebase apps like yours.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Summary & What's Next

You mastered Hooks: Rules (top level only, inside components), useState deep dive (object spread...user, array spread [...arr], functional update prev=>prev+1 for rapid changes), useEffect (side effects after render, []=mount once for Firebase fetch, [xp]=run when xp changes for auto-save, no array=every render), cleanup (return ()=>clearInterval for timers, removeEventListener, prevent memory leaks, isMounted flag for async fetch), useRef (box that doesn't trigger re-render, for DOM focus and render count).

blocks.question: MASTER APPLICATION: You need to build feature: When user opens React course page, fetch lessons from Firebase (once), show loading, start study timer that counts seconds, auto-save XP to localStorage whenever XP changes, and auto-focus search input. Which hooks and dependencies?
options: Only useState for everything
useState for lessons/loading/xp/timer, useEffect [] for fetch + focus, useEffect [] for timer with cleanup, useEffect [xp] for auto-save, useRef for search input focus
Use only useEffect with no dependencies
You need class components for this
blocks.correctFeedback: PERFECT! You just architected your real dashboard! That's exactly how your HTML file's Firebase logic works - useState + multiple useEffects with correct dependencies + useRef + cleanup. You are now job-ready for Hooks!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Break down: Fetch = useEffect [], Timer = useEffect [] + cleanup interval, Auto-save = useEffect [xp], Focus = useRef + useEffect [].
blocks.reasoning: Combining multiple hooks with correct dependencies is how real production dashboards like yours are built - this is Lesson 10 target foundation.
